---
title: "Where our evidence is thin: a tour of the weak spots"
description: "A paper is only as honest as the places it admits are soft. Here are ours."
author: "Yannick Loth"
date: "2026-10-15"
categories: [Self-correction, Metascience, Research]
---

It is easy to produce a confident-sounding document. It is harder — and more useful — to mark exactly where the confidence is not earned. Our paper tags speculative content with certainty values and flags weak-evidence areas; here is a plain-language tour.

**The soft spots:**

- **Single-study threads.** The norepinephrine story, the VMAT2/dopamine-circuit thread, and several others rest on a handful of small studies, sometimes from one group. Replication is pending.
- **Animal and cross-disease evidence.** Many mechanistic arrows (norepinephrine and clearance, norepinephrine and microglia, neuromodulators and cortical gain) are established in animals or other diseases, not measured in ME/CFS.
- **Composite measures.** New indices (like the norepinephrine "pathway index") are useful but unvalidated; a striking result can partly be an artefact of the measure.
- **Confounds that are not removed.** Deconditioning, medication, and activity level can all move the biomarkers we discuss, and most studies cannot rule them out.
- **The null and the negative.** Some of our strongest statements are about what does *not* work — amantadine for MS fatigue, GET, clonidine in adolescent CFS. Those deserve as much prominence as the positive ones.

**Why we flag them.** Because the alternative — a smooth narrative with the uncertainty sanded off — is how patients get misled, and how research priorities get set on air. A flag is not a weakness; hiding one would be.
